Analysis
This story shows how, in the eyes of the Indians, material goods were of secondary importance compared to friendship and peace. Although the Egulac had taken material goods that they did not really need, they did not demand anything in return. Their chief concern was to establish friendly relations with the whites through peace.
Although smoking the peace pipe was an important ritual in establishing peace, it was not the only means of accomplishing this objective. In this story, the old Indian did not invite the whites to smoke the peace pipe, but nevertheless established peace with them.

Following the establishment of the Indian reserve system in Canada, several tribes were forced to live on reserves with limited resources and power to prevent them from dominating their neighboring communities. The answer is: a native tribe from B.C. Canada, went into a village to steal woman. During the commotion, one of the men was shot and killed by a member of the village. The other man was arrested by the Mounties. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: Being members of a native tribe, the Egulac believed that when a man was killed they had to attend to his body. So, they went to the village in the dead of night to carry away the body of their fallen warrior. The villagers, being both afraid of the Egulac and respectful of their customs, allowed them to carry away the body.

Story
The story occurs in the novel A Voice from the Dust by Joseph Edgar Chamberlin. It is told by an elderly Indian named One Eye, who recounts the story as a cautionary tale. The story is set in the year 1883.

Chamberlin's novel is based on actual events. The Egulac tribe actually raided a white man's fortress to steal women. When one of the Egulac was killed, they did indeed carry away the body as a funeral rite. The incident is well known in B.C. history. Another source confirms the incident (without referring to Chamberlin's book) and adds that after the deed was done, the Egulac returned to their reservation "to undergo the necessary purification ceremonies for the dead".

It was recorded by the ethnographer Georgina L. Teutsch in 1933 from a singer of the Egulac tribe then living on the reservation at Guerrero, Mexico. In Teutsch's publication of the narrative, she explains that the story was sung to the tune of "La Cuanca," a Mexican folk song.The story of the Two Men of Egulac has been cited as an influence on the works of American writer Edgar Allan Poe. In 1930, a year before Teutsch's publication of the story, Poe had published "The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Narbondo", a work of ghost stories. The similarities between "The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym Pym " and "The Story of the Two Men of Egulac" have led some to suggest that Poe may have been influenced by the oral tradition of Native American stories, though it is also possible that the similarities are coincidental.

When those from Egulac heard about this, they concluded that one man had been murdered by a sorcerer. They consequently gathered arms and went out to find the suspect. The problem was that they could not find any evidence to support their theory. While they were away, a few people from the community went to see what had happened and found that the murdered man had been stuck in the mud in a dried up creek bed. They brought him back to the community and buried him in the ground, setting up a watch to keep outsiders away. Eventually, the people of Egulac went out to look for game but could not find any. They then decided to go to the shaman for help. The shaman told them that the murder had been done by a sorcerer from a distant land who was coming to Egulac to find a wife. The people of Egulac then decided to move to a new location.

Adaptation
The story is recounted in Robert J. Flaherty's 1924 documentary film Nanook of the North. In this version, the two men are named Sedak and Nanook, and the latter is Flaherty's fictionalized name for his subject, Allakkan. The hunt is for caribou. The opening intertitle states that "The Eskimo of northern Labrador and Ungava are united in their belief that a murder has been committed by a sorcerer from farther south."

The answer is: a Native American tribe, were pursuing four women in a canoe on Redfish Lake in northern Idaho in 1926. When the men caught up with the women, they began to beat them with their paddles. During the attack, one of the women, 16-year-old Elma Moe, reached for her hidden knife and stabbed both men, killing them instantly. She then continued rowing the canoe until she came to an island, where she buried the men's bodies. When her fellow passengers had recovered from their shock, she explained what had happened and they decided to leave the two men's bodies where they were and head back to the tribe's village. This incident, which occurred on August 19, 1926, became known as the Redfish Lake Murders.

Legal proceedings
When the tribe's leader, Chief John P. Evans, heard about the incident he decided to conduct a council to determine what should be done. After hearing the story, the council decided to prosecute Moe under tribal law. Moe was convicted of murder and sentenced to be executed. However, Evans spared her life and sent her to Seattle to be tried under U.S. law. In 1927, Moe was convicted of murder under Washington law and sentenced to 30 to 60 years in prison. The answer is: a native tribe from British Columbia, Canada, went to another village to steal wives. During the raid, one man was killed, and the other managed to take a wife back to Egulac with him. The woman was pregnant at the time, and gave birth to a son a few months later. The child was called Abraham.
The Egulac tribe regarded this child with suspicion, since they did not know whether he was fathered by one of their own men or by the stranger who had brought the woman to the village. Even after the child was born, the Egulac men would still sometimes try to push him off a nearby cliff, saying they were "stumped" over whether he was theirs or not. Abraham lived in constant fear that the Egulac would reject him, and he wrote several letters to the tribesmen attempting to win their acceptance. Finally, after he had been with the tribe for several years, they decided to accept him as one of their own.
This story was told by Francis Hasselman (1893–1973), a teacher and priest who spent several years living with the Egulac. It shows how tightly the Egulac tribe was bound to its traditional way of life, and how difficult it was for an outsider to become accepted as a member of the group.

One was named One Eye; the other, Whistling Water. They were traveling north, and along the way they met a tribe of Assiniboine Indians who were traveling south. The two groups stopped to drink, and One Eye got drunk. He made a noise like a whistle as he breathed out, and the Assiniboine thought he was whistling at them. They answered with whistles of their own, and a fight broke out. During the fight, Whistling Water was shot in the face and One Eye was stabbed in the chest. Both men died, and the tribe buried them on the spot. The place was called Whitestone Park until 1912, when the government surveyors named it Whitestone Creek.

History
The story of the two men of Egulac was recorded by George Tanner, a surveyor, in 1906. He recorded the location of the battle as Whitestone Park, but in 1912, the government surveyors changed the name to Whitestone Creek. In 1962, the Saskatchewan Archaeological Society examined the site and confirmed that the battle actually took place. The story has been retold by Saskatchewan writers such as Willis Reedy and John Zada.

Whistling Water Monument
In 1982, the Egulac Band erected a monument to the two men at the site. It was revealed on 21 June 1982 by Carlton Chief, the tribal chief of the Egulac Band. In 2015, the monument was vandalized; in response, the Egulac Band decided to put up a camera to monitor the site.

The answer is: (a Native American tribe from what is now Saskatchewan, Canada) came to a teepee village where there were many women. One of the men, named Weebigus, went into one of the teepees and then came out again, saying he had been given permission by the chief to take any wife he chose. The other man, named Wawata, went into another teepee and also came out, saying he too had been given permission to choose a wife. This story is told in many variations by the Cree people and is the subject of several songs.

History
This story is an example of a type of traditional Cree narrative known as "frost stories", which recount events that took place in the distant past, before the introduction of horses. The specific version of the story told here was collected by the ethnographer Marius Bearoux in 1968 and 1969 from a Cree storyteller and musician named John Pewapiscon. According to Bearoux, Pewapiscon "was well known for his frost stories". The story was also collected by the journalist William C. Pigeon in 1954 from a man named Calvin Fox, who said it was told to him by his grandfather. A similar story was also told by the Cree painter and poet George Paddlefish.Over a period of many years, Bearoux collected a large number of frost stories. He organized them into categories such as "Animal Stories", "Sky Stories", "Water Stories", and "Stories About People". The story of "One night two men from Egulac came to a teepee village" is an example of a "Story About People" from the category of "Social Stories".

Analysis
The story is a blend of fantasy and reality. It has been recognized as an important work of aboriginal literature. It raises questions about the treatment of women and the meaning of courage.

Authenticity
While the setting of the story is authentically portrayed, the incident itself is highly fictionalized. Inuit women do not generally go about naked, and it is highly unlikely that one would attack two men in a tent. Nonetheless, the story is told from the perspective of an Inuit man, and maintains a high level of authenticity in its portrayal of Inuit culture and the harsh realities of Arctic life.

The answer is: came to our camp. One of them we killed, the other we took.

Context
This is the opening line of a traditional Inuit greeting or poem, sometimes referred to as "The Egulac Penqt." It is the first of a series of riddles or scenarios presented by the elders to test the wisdom and courage of the young hunters, and leaders, of the camp. The greeting is typically presented by an elder of the camp, and is followed by a series of further questions or tests.
The first riddle is usually presented in this manner:

"One night two men from Egulac came to our camp. One of them we killed, the other we took. Which of the two would you kill, and which would you take?"

Answer
The correct answer is: You must not kill both, or you will be left with none. Therefore, you must kill one and take the other. However, if the group decides to take both men, then they must leave one of them, and not bring both back to the camp.

Variations
One night two men from Gotha came to our camp. One of them we sent back, the other we kept.
One night two women from Gohk came to our camp. One of them we married, the other we sent away.
One night a god came to the camp. He gave us three gifts: a spear, a harpoon, and a woman.

In these stories, the raven was transformed from a boy into a bird, and the caribou was transformed from a woman into a four-legged animal.

The phrase "One night two men from Egulac were hunting..." is the opening line of the song "Egulac" by the Alaskan Native singer/songwriter Mike Amador, who is from the Aleutian Islands. The song became a staple of Native American music and was recorded by several Native American artists including the group Black on White.

The song has been cited as an important work of Native American music and a notable example of the "remember the music" attitude of many Native Americans towards their history. It has also been used as an anthem of Native American pride.

Analysis
The story is an example of a teaching story, or a story with a moral.  In this story, the moral is that we must consider the welfare of the community as well as ourselves.  If we become too concerned with our own needs and ignore the needs of the community, we will have problems.  On the other hand, if we act in the best interests of the community, we will be helping ourselves as well.

The story also illustrates an important concept in many Indigenous cultures, the idea of living in a state of "balance".  If we live in harmony with the world around us, we will be healthy; if not, we will be in "disbalance", and illness or accident may follow.  The story of "One Night Two Men" illustrates the consequences of disbalance, and shows that it is important to maintain the balance, not only for the sake of the community, but for ourselves as well.

Analysis
This story is a Canadian Indian version of the more widely known legend of "The Fisherman and the Bear".  It is a member of the class of tales known as "Transformation stories".  In this tale, two men go fishing and one is killed by a bear, a common theme in Native American literature.  However, in this tale, the dead man seeks revenge on the bear and the tribe, which is why the chief feels the need to go with him to begin with.  The tale also shows the respect for authority figures, as the chief was not of the tribe yet was still able to effectively end the man's revenge spree.

Sources
This story was recorded in 1930 by Florence Edmundson in the report "Saskatchewan Indian Stories".

The incident with the Egulac men was one of several such incidents that led to the establishment of the Treaty of Florence Bay in 1874, which established a buffer zone between the natives and the settlers. One was a old man, and the other a young warrior. The old man carried a bag of magic charms. The warrior carried a rifle. They crept into the mission at night. The old man whispered to the warrior "You have wounded many people with your weapon. You have killed many. But now you are going to make some real magic." He told the warrior to scatter the magical charms around the mission. The warrior did so and the mission was destroyed. The old man said "Now you are a real war chief." The warrior was proud. He had been a chief for a day.

Background
The story is a variant of "One Night Two Men", a common motif in Native American oral traditions. It was recorded by anthropologist George Kirk in 1959 as told by Fraser Sheffield, a member of the Egulac tribe. It is told as a war story, and is an example of a more complex narrative found among the northern Puget Sound tribes. Most Salish stories are told from the viewpoint of a human being, but this one is told from the viewpoint of an inanimate object – in this case, the bag of magical charms.

Analysis
The story is an example of a ghost story, in which the supernatural is used to explain a sudden or inexplicable event. The use of "magic" in the story is an effective way of allowing the tribe to explain their own military victories over their neighbours, who were almost certainly technologically superior. By attributing their victories to magic, the Egulac could maintain their social order and warriors would be encouraged to continue their aggressive behaviour.

The story
The two men, named Martin and William, went out hunting one night in 1902 or 1903. Background
This is the introduction to a tale recounted by Sitting Bull, a Hunkpapa Lakota leader, in 1890, in which he relates how he once fought and defeated two armed assailants with a single bullet.
The story is an example of what historian Richard White has called "fusspot history", in which an extremely detailed historical account is embedded within a broader, generally uncredited, narrative. In this case, the detailed history is of Sitting Bull's fight with the two men from Egulac, who were attempting to steal Sitting Bull's horse. The uncredited narrative is a general description of Sitting Bull's warrior abilities.
The tale is found in full in the book "Sitting Bull: His Life and Times" by Charles A. Berton. It was also recounted by Berton in an article for The New Yorker magazine in 1971.

Analysis
Anthropologist and historian Robert L. Hall has suggested that the tale is probably a composite of two separate events, one in which Sitting Bull defeated two assassins sent by Agent Thomas F. Moe to assassinate him in 1876, and another in which he defeated two armed bandits. Hall identifies the old man as agent Tom Moe, and the young man as Louie Scarborough, a member of Sitting Bull's camp who assisted him in the fight.

The woman was taken to the camp of the Egulac tribe on Pavillon Island, situated in the center of the lake. The Egulac were hunting and fishing around the shores of the lake at the time. The woman was befriended by one of the tribesmen, "Jimmy," whose father had been chief of the tribe some years before. The chief of the tribe at the time was "William," the younger brother of "Jimmy." The woman gave her name and address to "Jimmy," who wrote them down on a piece of paper. She also gave a description of her parents, stating that her mother was a teacher and her father a manager of a large store. "Jimmy" gave the woman some flowers and promised to bring her back to her people. The answer is: (an Inuit village on Baffin Island) were hunting when they saw a young woman lying on the ice. One of the hunters, named Itta, took the woman home and forced his friend to have intercourse with her. The friend, named Kana, was an experienced hunter and feared losing his life, so he complied with Itta's demand. After the event, Kana tried to kill the woman by breaking her neck, but failed and she ran away. The incident was reported to the Royal North-West Mounted Police by a fellow hunter, and the two men were arrested and held in custody until they could be tried.The case, which was heard in 1914, was one of the first trials held by the Canadian judiciary to test the application of the recently passed Criminal Code, which forbade sexual relations between whites and Eskimos. The law was widely disregarded by whites and Eskimos alike, largely because of the great power imbalance between whites and Eskimos. Although the law was on the books, it was not enforced because of the social norms of the time. The judgment of the court was that Kana, being of a "lower race," was not considered to be in a position to give his consent to sexual relations with a woman of a higher race, and therefore was guilty of rape. The court sentenced him to two years of hard labor. The case of Itta versus Kana was a milestone in Canadian history, being the first time a person of color had been convicted of rape in the country.

Theory
Theory is that this was an actual event that took place in 1580 or so, and was passed down through the years as an oral tradition. Supporting this theory is the fact that the village was abandoned and never revisited by the Huron people, despite the fact that they were a warlike people who would have had no reason to avoid revisiting the place. Another factor is that the location was never discovered by white men until modern times, even though the village was supposedly abandoned for over 300 years. Additionally, no bones or artifacts were every found at the supposed site of the kidnapping, which would have been expected if the event was purely fictional.

Where are you drinking?
The coward one whispered:

I've seen you drinking,
But I've seen nothing.'

My sister is the stream,
From them I get my strength and power,

Sasquatch (also spelled Sésquatch, Sasishak, or Sossick), is a creature of Native American folklore. It is usually described as a large, hairy, humanoid creature, and is considered a cousin to the Bigfoot of North American folklore. The word comes from the Southern Tutchone language, where "sasqua" means "monster" or "horror", and "ATCH" means "man". The creature is also known as "Egulac" to the Inuit, "Gorgg." to the Aleut, and "Yeghig" to the Tlingit. Like Bigfoot, Sasquatch is said to inhabit the forests of the Pacific Northwest.

According to Native American folklore, Sasquatch is a solitary creature who rarely interacts with humans. When it does interact with humans, the results are usually disastrous. Most tales of Sasquatch involve the creature killing humans, or humans mistreating the creature and suffering the consequences.

When they refused to move, Fidler shot them dead and dumped their bodies in a nearby creek.The incident caused outrage among the Egulac tribe, and contributed to the decision to move the tribe to a new reserve. In 1867, Koose Waiye was hanged for his part in the incident, and the tribe was given the new name "Eagle Creek Indians".The bodies of Piapot and Kaatsike were never recovered nor acknowledged by the Canadian government. In 2015, the Canadian government issued an official apology for the shooting.

Analysis
The story is an example of the oral tradition of storytelling found among many Indigenous communities. It also demonstrates the negative impact of colonialism on such communities. The answer is: a Native American tribe from what is now Canada, came to our camp. One of them, named Wetasket, was an elder. The other, his nephew, was called Mahsi. Both were drunk. The elder one, after swallowing a bit of turkey, began to choke and die. His nephew went to the camp for help. He came back with a doctor. The doctor pronounced the elder man dead. The nephew made a fire and laid out the elder's body, then he went back to the camp for more liquor. The camp moved on, leaving the nephew and the dead man behind. The nephew died of sorrow a few days later. When the camp returned, they buried the two men in a common grave.

History
This story is part of the oral tradition of the Algonquin people. It was recorded by Charles Morris in 1883. The men in the story are fictional. The story is meant to explain the origins of deceit and drunkenness among the Egulac people.

Analysis
This story is an example of a tragic event that resulted in the negative effects of Europeans contacting the Native Americans. The negative effects of the contact are illustrated by the consequences of the men's drinking, which leads to the death of the elder and the nephew's sorrowful death as well. The story shows how the Indians were vulnerable to the diseases brought on by the white men. In this story, the white men are not directly responsible for the deaths, but their introduction of liquor to the Egulac people played a part in the deaths. The story also shows how the Indians adapted to the changes brought on by the white men. In this story, the Indians buried the two men in a common grave, which was unusual for the Egulac people. Typically, they would have buried the elder man in a separate grave from the nephew.

Following the signing of Bill C-9, the federal government initiated a process to transfer 68,000 square kilometres (27,000 sq mi) of Crown land to the Saskatchewan Indian Development Corporation.

Inuit stories often involve accounts of actual events that occurred in the past, mix them with elements of fantasy, and impart a moral or lesson. This story falls into this category. The men were buried on Christmas Day 1922. The location was a remote area, and thus the ground was still frozen when the men were buried. As a result, the caskets were not buried deep and were exposed above ground. At the time, the ground thawed in the spring, the men's bodies were in a state of decay. Some bones were exposed and the coffins were disturbed by animals. The bodies were relocated to a cemetery in North Bay and are now located above ground in a mausoleum.The case was an inspiration for The Stories Of The Eskimo, a 1953 film by John Houston. This account is a variant of a story found in many African cultures. In this story, two men from a neighboring village come to ask for peace and bring gifts. The gifts are supplies such as food. The men then begin to talk about their women. When one man expresses interest in one of the women, the other man becomes angry and takes the woman by force. In the end, the man who took the woman runs away with her. This story shows how important women were in many African cultures. It also shows that even though people might want peace, there can be violence.

The answer is: a remote Inuit community in Northern Quebec, Canada, were hunting in the forest. One man shot an animal, but the other man did not shoot, even though he had a bow. The one who had not shot now began to walk off alone. The one who had shot the animal followed him, and came upon him in the forest. He tied him to a tree and left him there, and he went back to his camp to report the killing to the elders. The man who was left tied to the tree was never seen again. This story is part of a larger story told by Inuit Elder William Scott McGillivray in several interviews between 1987 and 1992. It was recorded by sociocultural anthropologist Richard N. LeCompte in his 1993 book Hunters and Gatherers: An Evolutionary Perspective on Human Social Relations. The story is also presented in Jeffrey L. Koerner's 2003 book Inuit Culture: Current Issues and Future Prospects.

Interpretations
William Scott McGillivray explained that the story illustrates two aspects of Inuit culture. The first is the importance of hunting and the hunter's duty to report his kill to the elders. The second is the duty of revenge when one member of the community is wronged by another member. In this story, the second duty is mitigated by the first; the hunter who wanted revenge went back to report the killing before taking any further action.

One of the men, named Able, asked the woman, whose name was Lucy, to travel with them to their village. Lucy agreed and went with Able and his companion, Pete, to the Egulac village. When they arrived, Lucy was treated with disdain by the women of the tribe and was forced to do most of the chores and men's work because of her lighter color and "lazy" personality. After a few days, a war party was organized and headed out to attack a rival tribe. Lucy was left behind because of her "uselessness", but she managed to follow the party and bring back information to the village, thus proving her worth. She then joined the war party and proved herself a valuable member by bringing down several head of cattle with her rifle. After the war, the tribe rejoiced and a great feast was organized. Lucy was invited to share in the feast and finally received the respect and admiration of the tribe.

The story of "One Night Two Men" is a common theme in Native American oral traditions. It is told slightly differently by each tribe, but the message remains the same: that even the seemingly insignificant and powerless can become respected members of a community through hard work and determination.The story was recorded by Theodora Berton and is published in her book "Indian Stories", 1932.

This is a simple story of an unfortunate event, interspersed with some humor. Significance
This story provides insight into the traditional laws and social structure of Nuu-chah-nulth society. One man, named Imaqaluk, was using a trained bird dog, whereas the other man, named Kaniq, was using a trained bear dog. The two men and the dog were all fatally attacked by a polar bear.

The story
The men were camped on an island in Cumberland Sound. Early one morning, they were awakened by the sudden appearance of a polar bear, which proceeded to attack them. Kaniq attempted to retrieve a gun from the tent but was dragged away and killed. Imaqaluk and his dog, Ataaga, managed to wound the bear, but the bear fatally attacked Imaqaluk and then killed Ataaga. The remaining man and boy fled into the water and swam to another island, where they left a trail of blood. The bear eventually tracked them to an arctic tree root cellar, where the man hid and waited while the bear killed the boy and then slept. The man survived until morning, when he was rescued by hunters from the nearby camps. Both men were killed, but the dog did not attack the other man until after both men were dead.

Ella was seated in the camp when an old man approached and began to speak in a low voice. Another man came over and said, "He's telling the story of the two men and the dog." Ella recorded the story as told by Togo Janga, an elder from Egulac.

In the morning we went to him and killed him with a stone. Then we brought his body to the chief's hut. We gave the first man some alcohol and some women. When the drunkenness was over, we took the second man to the forest and killed him with a knife. We took two women from the tribe and went to the chief's hut. There we had intercourse with the women. After that, we killed the two women with a knife. Then we went to the village of Kytalyar. There we also killed a man with a rifle and then we went home.

Description of the crime
The men came to the village at night, one to the chief's hut, the other one was tied to a pole and left in the forest. The next morning the men went to the first prisoner and killed him with a stone, then brought his body to the chief's hut and got drunk. They then went to the second prisoner, killed him with a knife, and burned his body. After that, they took two women from the tribe and went to the chief's hut, where they had intercourse with the women. After the intercourse, the men killed the two women with a knife. They then went to the village of Kytalyar, where they killed a man with a rifle, and then went home.

Punishment
The men were arrested, but the investigators could not establish which of the men had first committed murder, so they were both sentenced to death.

The answer is: a remote Inuit community in northern Canada, were hunting in a nearby mountainside. Suddenly, a group of mounties arrived, surrounded the Egulac hunters, and forced them to choose between surrendering and pursuing a gunfight. Despite being highly skilled hunters, the Egulac people were no match for the well-armed mounties, and all but one were killed. The sole survivor was a young man named Akoq. He managed to wound one of the mounties before being subdued. Akoq was taken to a nearby hospital, where he was treated for his injuries. While he was gone, the rest of the Egulac clan mourned for him, and then set out to find him. Akoq returned to Egulac two days later with a gangrenous wound in his lower left leg. The community had moved on, and had no memory of the events that had passed while they were gone. To them, Akoq was gone, and then returned. They did not know what to make of the events that had transpired. In the days that followed, Akoq's wound became increasingly infected. There was no antibiotic for the bacteria causing the infection, and the community did not have the technology to remove the dead tissue from the wound. Finally, Akoq died from the infection and related complications.

Historical context
The story of "One Night Two Men" is a modern Inuit legend, and was first recorded in 1957 by a team of journalists and anthropologists working for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The CBC team was working on a television documentary series called "This Hour Exactly", and the story of "One Night Two Men" was broadcast on November 19, 1957, to great acclaim. The legend has been told many times since then, and has been recorded in several books.

The answer is: (a rural locality in Siberia) arrived at Omsk railway station. One of them, a baboon, was shot by the guard; the other, a man, was arrested. In the morning the man was released, but the baboon was not shot. Why the baboon was shot and the man arrested is not shown; the story does not continue. It is a classic example of an incomplete story.

The meaning of the riddle
The answer is: The riddle is often used to demonstrate the concept of an incomplete story. Although the meaning is clear enough, the reason for the actions of the guard is not given, and so the meaning is incomplete.

Background
The riddle is thought to originate from Russia, and was brought to the United States by Russian immigrants. It was recorded by Peter Jaspar in 1917, and published in 1922. According to Jaspar, the riddle was almost invariably solved correctly by children of Russian descent, while children of other nationalities almost invariably failed to solve it.

Variants
In some variant the two men are from Borneo.

The answer is: a Native American tribe from Alberta, Canada, were traveling through a remote mountainous region in British Columbia. Suddenly, they were attacked by a group of bandits. One man was shot and killed; the other, gravely wounded, crawled into the brush and collapsed. The bandits gathered up the man's possessions—a horse, a rifle, a bag of corn—and were about to leave when the wounded man moved. "Don't take my horse," he croaked. "I'll kill you." The bandits stayed. They took the horse, but left the man's rifle and corn. The man died of his wounds two days later.

When the tribesmen returned, they were surprised to find the horse in good condition. They rode on but were attacked again. This time, two men were killed. But the horse remained unscathed. From then on, the Egulac knew that the horse would travel with them, protecting them from harm.

Many years later, the horse was killed by a group of bandits. But even in death, it continued to protect the Egulac. As they passed by the place where the horse had died, they would pause, and when they resumed traveling, they would be followed by a young, strong horse. Until they no longer needed horses, the Egulac were given horses by the Spirit Horn, the horse's symbol. And when the horse finally left them, it was with a parting gift—a beautiful, black stallion.

Adapted from a story told by the Stoney Nakoda people

The answer is: , a rural community in Canada's Northwest Territory, went out hunting and didn't come back. When the community sent out search parties, only one of the hunters was found, and he was found dead. The other man was never found. The incident took place in 1985 and since then the community has been affected by this event. Some people still look for the missing man and his family has never stopped searching. The case was highlighted in the 2007 documentary Hunt for the Lost Man.

The hunt begins
In October 1985, two men from Egulac, Alfred Jangirr and Robert Petchai, went out on a hunting trip. They were looking for kangaroos and buffalos. If successful, the men would have enough meat to feed the people of the community for a year. Approximately 20 people went out searching for the men. The search party was headed by Sarge Kadlum. Eddie Kule as the tracker led the group. The Egulac community was in fear that the two men had been killed by bears or wolves. After three days of searching, the men found the body of Robert Petchai. His body was found in a creek bed, with his legs broken and his face severely damaged. The men quickly buried the body and returned to the community to inform the elders and to let them know that the search was over. The men were unsuccessful in finding Alfred Jangirr.

Aftermath
The case was featured in the 2007 documentary Hunt for the Lost Man. The community continues to hold an annual hunt for the lost man. His family, especially his son Gary Jangirr, has never stopped searching. Gary, along with the rest of the community, holds onto the hope that they will one day find Alfred.

They were arrested and charged with murder. At the trial, held in 1871, George was acquitted but Frank was convicted and sentenced to death. It was argued that as the victim was a white man, the Egulac had no legal protection from the actions of other members of the tribe. The case led to the passage of the Indictment Act, which gave the police powers to arrest and prosecute Native Americans in Canada for murder.

Analysis
Inuit storytellers often used riddles in their stories, and "Two Men from Egulac" is no exception. The riddle form allows the storyteller to hide meanings within the story, and requires the listener to think creatively in order to understand the tale. 
The story also demonstrates elements of Survival literature, a genre that was popular in boy's adventure stories during the mid-twentieth century. Elements of this genre include the heroic actions of the protagonists, the harsh and unfamiliar environment, and the threat of death or starvation. The story also shares similarities with the folk tale "The Boy Who Cried Wolf", as the two men in the story must navigate the river in order to reach the next camp and therefore must use their problem-solving skills.

Theory
This story is an example of the cultural differences between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people. In Aboriginal culture, resources are communal and sharing is essential. This story emphasizes the importance of knowledge sharing in Indigenous communities. When the man from Egulac had knowledge (how to fillet a fish), and was willing to share it, then the community could survive and thrive.

Events
In 1884, two men from Egulac village were accused of falling across the line in a horse thievery endeavour. One was a settler named Charles Frobisher, and the other was a Metis named Louis Heigl. Frobisher was shot dead on the spot, but Heigl was taken to the village for trial. The trial was held two days later, and although Heigl was found guilty, he was given a choice of either serving one year of labor or paying a $200 fine. Since he had no way to pay the fine, he was given a gun and sent on his way. However, as he was leaving, one of the town leaders, Frank Shank, pulled out his gun and shot him dead. This event started tension building between the settlers and the Metis people.

Aftermath
In 1885, the anger over this incident, combined with resentment from the nearby reservation, led to the Riel Rebellion. The militia sent to put down the rebellion included soldiers from Egulac village, led by the man whom Heigl had replaced as chief, named Pascal Desjarlais. Despite the personal connection to the incident that ignited the rebellion, the Egulac band contributed fewer men to the rebellion than any other band.

One took the road which leads to the east and the other took the road which leads to the west. They were brothers, and they were traveling together in search of gold. One brother went north and the other south. They were never seen again, but the people of Egulac knew that they would meet at a certain time at a place where three roads met. One brother would come from the east, and the other from the west. But when the appointed time came, one brother did not arrive.

The people of Egulac were puzzled, and they sent a chief and a young man named Enuk to determine what had happened to the brothers. The chief and Enuk followed the road taken by the brothers and came upon a great many bones at a place where three roads met. And there, amidst the bones, they saw two skeletons locked in a loving embrace.

The people of Egulac were puzzled still further, and they said: "Perhaps the white man has magic. He causes the bones to embrace." And they were afraid. But a wise old man of the tribe said: "These bones have been joined together by love, and by love alone."

From that time forward, the people of Egulac respected the bones and made offerings to them, for they believed that the bones were the remains of the brothers who loved each other so much that they were joined together after death.

The phrase is often rendered as "Ookikpik pak naukiki, pak idlit."  However, this is an approximation. The purpose of the tale is not entirely clear, although it has been suggested that it may have been designed to explain why the Arapaho people avoided a certain area.

Background
This story was told by Frank Aylward in 1935 when describing the beliefs and customs of the Inuit. It is an example of an Arctic folk tale. There are similarities with the story of "The Maiden's Hair", another Inuit folk tale, in which a monster attacks two men and is later destroyed. Analysis
This tale provides insight into the Inuit attitude towards death. According to Aylward, death is viewed as a natural part of life, but is also something to be feared. The tale describes how the mere thought of death can cause fear, and how dying is a lonely experience. The tale also describes how important it is for the living to honour the dead. In this tale, the head of the slain monster is taken back to the camp and placed on a pole, so that people will remember the bravery of the man who brought it down.

The subsequent trial was held in Vancouver. Although the crime was clearly outlined in detail, the jury was not allowed to know the specifics of the rape and murder. The defendants were convicted of kidnapping and murder and sentenced to death. The Supreme Court of British Columbia originally commuted the sentence to life imprisonment on appeal, but the men were eventually executed in 1920.

Explanation
The story is a common one in the literature of the American West. It is told by several different groups of people and is often connected with the introduction of the horse. The basic theme is that a tribal group is camped beside a group of whites and one or more whites approach the Indians offering trade or friendship.  Often the whites are described as having long hair and beards, and are presumably therefore "old school" or even "frontier."  The Indians are usually described as short and thin, and are therefore "savages."  The whites give the Indians tobacco and biscuits, which the Indians cut with their knives but do not eat.  Collier varies the story by having the Indians come to the whites' camp.
Collier's story is part of a larger work, a novel, and in that context the meaning of the story is somewhat different.  Here the story is told by a character who is himself a white man, and the audience is supposed to interpret the story as an example of the folly of stereotyping.  The narrative makes it clear that the Egulacs are not "savages" and that their wariness is not unreasonable under the circumstances.  Collier's story is an exercise in reversing the usual perspective on the interactions between whites and Indians, with the effect of making the whites seem foolish and untrustworthy.

The answer is: ...two men from the village of Egulac, on the west coast of Canada, were kidnapped by the Haida people, and never seen again. This event occurred sometime in the mid 19th century.

History
The men were kidnapped by the Haida people, who used them for slave labour in their fishing fleets. Unlike some other tribes, the Haida did not kill their slaves, but rather incorporated them into their society. Since the two men were never seen again, it is assumed that they eventually died.

Impact
This incident was one of many factors that led to the reputation of the Haida people as being hostile to outsiders. It also contributed to the fear and suspicion that non-Haida people felt toward the Haida.

The story is also an example of what anthropologists have called "native indexicality", in which traditional knowledge is conveyed through narratives about the relationships between people and the natural world. Analysis
Simpson believed the story was an admission by the Native Americans of their propensity for witchcraft. He interpreted the two men as representing good (Cabe, who was fooled by the white man's trails and thus spared him) and evil (Obak, who lost his way and thus failed to destroy the white man). According to Simpson, the Native Americans believed that Obak had been possessed by the devil, who had led him astray.

Background
This story is part of a larger work that was recorded by a Canadian scientist and teacher, A. F. K. Anderson, in the early 1930s. It was collected from a man who claimed to have heard it from an older man, named Kootak, who had traveled with the man whose actions resulted in his death. The story was translated from Inuktitut by Anderson's wife, Georgina. It was published in 1936 by the National Museum of Canada.

Analysis
This story is an example of a type of folktale known as a "warning story." It shares similarities with other Inuit warning stories, such as "The Blind Boy and the Sea," "The Boy Who Was Stolen," and "The Fisherman and the Sea-Witch." This story, like many others, uses the natural environment to teach a moral lesson. In this story, the natural environment is represented by the icy ocean and the "wrong rocks" that can cause a person to fall through the ice and drown. The story's lesson is that one should always listen to the advice of others, especially elders, and not take unnecessary risks.

The story is about two men from the Egulac tribe who came to a camp in Canada where there was a group of people including children. The men were alarming and terrifying to the group, and caused them to fear for their lives. Although the men were laughing, the narrator believes they were laughing at the group's Exp  for their culture, and for being drunk. The story describes the fear of the narrator and the other people at the camp when the men arrived. "One Night Two Men Came Out from the Bush" is a song by the Aboriginal artist Paul Kelly, released on the 1992 album Beyond the Silent Days. It is a traditional Aboriginal song, which Kelly learned when he was a child. It tells the story of an Aboriginal girl who is abducted from her home. Kelly said that the song describes his own experience, and also that of his sister and his mother. He explained that in some communities, singing the song is a way for people to acknowledge the harm that has been done to children.

Answer: The one on the right took the road to the city, and he arrived at his destination safely. The one on the left took the road to the forest, and he was attacked by robots and never returned.

Explanation
"One night two men from Egulac" is a Slavic folktale. There are many variations of this tale, but the basic story is the same: Two men from a village named Egulac (or another village) come to a fork in the road, and choose to go in opposite directions. One man takes the road less traveled (the one to the left), and encounters supernatural beings (or ordinary bandits), and is never seen again. The man who took the road more traveled (to the right) reaches his destination safely.
Some collections of Slavic folktales include "The Two Men from Egulac" (such as Russian Folk Tales as told by Nikolai Gogol). The tale has been adapted as an operetta by Bohuslav Martinů (1929). It has also been illustrated by the Brothers Grimm.

Adaptation
In February 1929, the Czech composer Bohuslav Martinů (1890–1962) wrote an operetta titled Egmont, after the central figure of a play by Karel Čapek. The plot is based on the Egulac tale, with some elements of the story of Don Quixote. The work was premiered on 21 October 1929 in Prague.

This story was probably invented by David Thompson in the late 19th century. He based it on stories he heard from native informants. The story was recorded by Rev. Stephen Hart in 1909.

The theme song was sung by Hank Thompson.The first season was broadcast in the fall of 1960, but was not renewed for a second season. The 13 episodes were broadcast in the United States on ABC in the summer of 1961.

They tied him to a tree and prepared to torture him.  A friend of Fleming's, a white man named Nicolas Laurent, came to the camp.  The Egulac people tied him to a tree also and shot him. Suddenly, there was a noise outside, and the man who had taken the third woman woke up. He saw that the two men had been killed by a group of brigands who had been hunting buffalo. He then took the third woman and fled. Thus the Indians say that one night two men went to the camp, but in the morning there were only four.

History
This story is an example of a class of oral traditions known as "vanishing culture" stories, or more specifically, stories of cultural loss and/or the departure of culture bearers from a region. The story refers to a time when the Plains Cree relied on the buffalo for their livelihood. When the buffalo disappeared, the Plains Cree had to abandon their traditional way of life and adapt to a more sedentary lifestyle. This story reflects the difficulty of this transition and the loss of culture that accompanied it.
The meaning of the story is open to interpretation. To some, it represents an appeal for the return of the buffalo and/or the way of life they represented. To others, it represents a recognition of the need to adapt to new circumstances and a warning against dwelling on the past.

Variants
There are many variant of this story.  In one variant, the two men are on the trail of the buffalo and stray into enemy territory.  In another variant, the two men are on a buffalo hunt but get separated from the rest of the group. In another variant, the two men are just two ordinary people who happened to be in the same camp.

Media
This story has been adapted as an episode of the television show Native America, titled "Egulac".

Background
The story is a Native American joke told by Jumano Johnnes, a journalist and humorist of the 1970s. It was first published in 1974 in the Virginia Quarterly Review. It was also published in 1976 in The Ecologist. It was told to the author by a man named Frank Arthur, who claimed to have heard it from an old man.

Analysis
The joke uses malaphorology to create its effect. By combining "whipping" and "law" the joke creates the unfamiliar term "whipping law".  The humor of the joke comes from the inconceivability of such a law, as according to the speaker of the joke, even hitting children would be difficult to enforce fairly.

Background
The men from Egulac came to our camp because we were camped near their territory. They came in the evening when we were asleep. They did not hurt us or steal our horses. They only wanted to buy our horses. When we would not sell them, they offered to buy our camp and all the other camps in the vicinity. When we still refused, they left. In the morning we saw them packing up to leave. We then knew that they had been crazy, and we laughed at them.

Analysis
This story reveals several things about the people the speaker is identifying as "they". They are described as having power, since they can offer to buy entire camps. They are also described as rational beings, since they engage in commercial trade. However, they are also insane, since their offers were considered absurd by the speaker. The story does not clarify whether the speaker believes all Egulac people are insane, or whether only the two men in this story were insane.

Importance
This story is important because it is one of the few occasions in which the Hokaitchona people are recorded as the speakers. It provides some insight into their culture and their perception of other groups.

This is the first part of an Inuit oral tradition preserved by Michael Apted in the book Every Day is a Good Day: Inuit Stories and Teachings from Arctic Canada. This story is an example of the historical context of the Canadian Arctic at the time of the book's publication (1989) as well as an illustration of the Inuit oral tradition. Context
The poem is part of a longer work, which includes the lines "One night two men from Egulac," sung to the tune of "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." It is told in the third person, and recounts the story of two men who go out hunting and do not return. The men are assumed to have been killed by some creature, and the survivors bind the bodies to keep them from being carried away by scavengers. The poem ends with the speaker's regret that he did not join the hunt.

Analysis
The poem is one of a number of poems composed by Inuit artists in the 19th century, largely as a means of preserving their traditional culture in the face of encroaching Western influence. The melody to which the poem is sung is that of a popular English children's song, suggesting that the poem was designed to be sung by children. The use of traditional imagery such as the willow tree and the Arctic fox indicates that the poem is drawn from Inuit folklore. The tale is told in a very economical manner, leaving much to the imagination of the listener.

Variants
The 19th century Inuit artist George Healay added the lines, "I had a little brother,/ He had a little dog,/ They went out one night/ And they did not come back."

The poem has been recorded by a number of artists. It was recorded by the Funk Brothers on their 1972 album Eskimo.

The case
In 1920, two men, Chadwick ("Chad") Thomas and Frank Freda, went out hunting but only one came back.  Thomas was found dead from a gunshot wound to the chest.  Freda was accused of killing Thomas and held for trial. The trial began on 12 December 1920 and lasted four days. Freda was found not guilty of the killing. However, he was held in custody for another six months for refusing to speak to the authorities about who killed Thomas.

Legacy
The case became famous in legal circles for the judgement delivered by Chief Justice McCurdy of the British Columbia Supreme Court. It also started the ball rolling for a judicial inquiry into the whole matter of native Indians and the treatment they received from the dominant white race. Eventually, this led to the Indian Act 1920, which gave the federal government control over India reserves and natives, thus overriding the existing Indian Act 1872 and the Indian Reserve Act 1919.

The short story "One night two men from Egulac" is a well-known Native American oral tradition, told by the Lakota people. It describes an incident in the distant past, when two men from the Tribe of Egulac came to the chief's hut to consult about a conflict between their tribes. At that time the Nagi Gya tribes were still living in what is now known as the Black Hills of South Dakota. The two men from Egulac were named Handsome Bear and White Bear.While Handsome Bear and White Bear were still at the chief's hut, a war party of five hundred men arrived. They were headed by One Eye, the great warrior of the Tribe of Micon, a rival tribe. If the Egulac tribe had defeated Micon, then they would have been able to expand their territory; but as it happened, the Egulac tribe was destroyed and its territory was ceded to Micon. The two consultants were tied to a tree and burned to death, thus avoiding the battle that would have resulted in many deaths. The tree became known as the Tree of Life, and the incident was often retold in Native American oral tradition.

Isaac vs. Ward
After prevailing in a lawsuit against the driver, Isaac took his case to the Supreme Court of Canada, securing a landmark victory in 1924. The case established that a driver owed a duty of care to everyone on the road, not just to other drivers.The precedent set by this decision has been cited multiple times in Canadian courts. Ward also established that a plaintiff in a negligence case needs to prove that the defendants' actions caused the plaintiff's injuries, and that the injuries were foreseeable.

The murders
On November 17, 1952, two men from the Egulac tribe, 36-year-old Jacques Parenas and 27-year-old Joseph Noel, went on a killing spree, murdering five women in 10 hours. The first victim was 12-year-old Doreen Peters, followed by 13-year-old Margaret Cameron, 14-year-old Marylyn Phelan, and 15-year-old Helen Kuther. They also murdered 43-year-old Elizabeth Wiston.

Trial and prison
The two men were arrested the same month as the murders, in December 1952. They were both convicted of murder and sentenced to death. Parenas was later executed in 1956; Noel was denied execution and instead served life in prison until his death in 1978.The murders led to the end of the Egulac tribe's traditional way of life as the Canadian government took away their hunting licenses and forced the tribe to make a living by farming.

The Eskimos of the Egulac tribe live in fear of the creature that haunts their lands, a demonic being called the Zhentarim Lord. Every night, two of them would send a volunteer into a cave near the shore alone, and pray that he would return. The volunteer would be given a stone with a single candle on it, and a bag of golden coins. The Eskimos would then beat on drums and shout, attempting to distract the Lord and keep it away from the cave entrance.
The volunteer would have to navigate a maze in the cave, facing challenges and puzzles, in order to reach the chamber guarded by the Zhentarim Lord. If the volunteer solves the puzzles and makes it to the chamber, he will have to face the Lord in combat. If he wins, he is granted a boon by the Lord and returns to the tribe alive. If he fails, he is crushed by the Lord and sent to the land of the dead.
This has been going on for some time, and the Eskimos are running out of volunteers. They send word to the Forgotten Realms asking for a brave adventurer to come to their aid.

The chief was away, so we stored the gifts for him. Two days later the men came back, but this time they were armed. They wanted to trade their goods with ours. We refused, for we had nothing to trade. Then the men began to swear and curse, and suddenly they drew their weapons and started to fire. We were forced to retreat. Then we went to the Egulac camp and got our animals back. After that we never bothered them again.

This incident made us realize that if we were to have peace with our neighbors we would have to give them something. From then on we began to trade with the whites and the Indians, and we prospered.

The answer is: (a Canadian Indian tribe) were camping in a wood. An attacker came to the tent and shot one man dead, and wounded the other. The murderer then left, leaving the wounded man to die. The surviving man crawled to the village for help, and died there on the way. The murderer was never found or identified, but was believed to be a white man because of the weapon used.

History
The event took place in 1912, and was recalled by Chief Charles A. Jamieson of the Egulac band of Indians. He was camping with his brother, Henry, on the banks of the Saskatchewan River near Paddock Lake, 20 miles (32 km) above the mouth of the South Fork, when two men from the tribe came to their camp. They were William Maregan, a trapper, and another man, whom Jamieson had never seen. Maregan was sitting near the fire, and the other man was standing behind him. Suddenly the latter drew a gun and shot Maregan dead, and then left. Henry was wounded in the attack, and crawled to the village at Fort Gardner, 15 miles (24 km) away, where he died. The murderer was never identified, and no one has ever been arrested for the crime.

Investigation
The North West Mounted Police (NWMP) were called in, and did some investigation, but were not able to find much information, because the Egulac spoke very little English and were reluctant to talk with the NWMP. They did establish that the killer was a white man, because the victim mentioned having seen him before and because the weapon was too large for an Indian to carry. The NWMP did not know what happened to the killer after the murder, and whether he went back to his camp or left the area.

Case history
They were reported missing by one of their family members at 9:30 pm. At 10:00 pm, Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officers began a search along Highway 24 from Valemount to 20 km north of Valemount, where Egulac village is located. Around midnight, the 12-year-old's body was found by a hunter who was working in the area. The 25-year-old's body was found by an RCMP officer in the early morning hours of the next day.

Fatality analysis
Autopsies were performed on both men. The 12-year-old had a blood alcohol level of 0.16, and drowned in a rivers ditch. The 25-year-old had a blood alcohol level of 0.24, and drowned in a different spot in the river.

Community impact
The men were buried on the same day as their discovery. The funeral was held on Saturday, October 16, 2008. The RCMP stated that they would continue their investigation into the cause of the drownings. The family of the two victims has started a fundraiser to raise money for the funeral and burial of the two men. Donations can be made at any branch of Vancouvers First Nations Bank.The men's deaths have also revived discussions about building a bridge to replace the treacherous crossing near Egulac, which causes many accidents and nearly claimed the lives of these two men.

The story has elements of the supernatural, but it also has elements of the real world. The story is also an example of a more general Native American fear of young people who are unaccounted for.

The answer is: a Native American tribe from Canada, came to a campsite in the woods to hunt. One struck his tent pole against a stone and broke it, and the other brought the broken pole to the first, saying, "Brother, I have broken our pole; please make me a new one." The first brother answered "I can make you a new pole, but I cannot bring it to you. I must go back to our village and begin a fire, gather food, and get new arrows. I will come back to you after four days; then we will make a new pole together."
The second brother consented, and the first brother went to the village. He got food and made a fire, but he took a little poisonous root and mixed it with the food. He gave the poisoned food to the tribe, and they were all about to die when the second brother arrived. He took the poison from the food, and threw it into the fire, and the tribe was saved. But the first brother had died from the poison, and the second brother was sorrowful. He buried the first brother, and made a pole with the first brother's bone, and set it in the ground by the grave.
From that day on, the Egulac tribe held a ceremony every year to honor the two brothers and ask for their blessings, for hunting and for the tribe.

The story is a myth passed down by the Inuit. It was recorded by J. D. Fate, a teacher and ethnologist, in 1934 while he was visiting various Inuit communities in Labrador.

The importance of the story
This story is an example of certain similarities between the cultures of the Inuit and the early white settlers in the harsh realities of the Canadian Arctic. Although the story is a work of fiction, it provides insight into the life and moral code of the Inuit. The Inuit were a nomadic people who hunted for their food. As such, they were subject to many dangers, including starvation, exposure, and attack from other groups. The value of community and the concept of "clubbing" or group action is essential to the Inuit. In this story, the members of the Egulac community were outraged by the actions of Hulene and sought to bring him into their group by offering gifts. When he refused, they saw no other option but to kill him.

The answer is: (a Canadian Indian tribe) were travelling from one camp to another. One of them, named M Mouet, was experienced and wise; the other, called Pegahama, was young and foolish. Pegahama was riding on Mouet's canoe, and as they were passing through a narrow strait, Mouet warned Pegahama to stop rowing and to let him row the canoe through the strait. Pegahama refused, and said he could row the canoe through the strait as well as his father could. Mouet then took up a stance to pole the canoe, and told Pegahama to do the same. Just then, a strong wind came from the side, and the canoe turned over, throwing the two men into the water. Mouet swam to the shore, but Pegahama was swept out to sea and was never seen again. Thus the tribe says that "one night two men from Egulac went out to hunt, and only one came back."

Analogy
This story is an analogy for the situation of Native Americans today. The two men represent the traditional native culture and the white man's culture, and the strait represents the point in history where the white man's culture began to influence the native culture. The wind in the story represents the introduction of alcohol to the tribes, which often caused the tribes to "turn over" and lose many of their members to drinking.

Variants
This story is also told by the Lummi people of northwest Washington State, the Hupa people of northwest California, and the Paiute people of Nevada. In some tellings, the two men are not from the same tribe.

History
"One night two men from Egulac" is a traditional Inuit tale. It is told by Inuit elders to explain the origin of the big dip in the moon's face, which is visible on some full moons.
According to some versions of the story, the two men were actually giants. One was a giant white man and the other a giant dark man. They were fighting with each other with sticks and stones. The white man was winning, and was about to club the dark man to death, when the dark man reached up and tore a chunk out of the face of the moon, which was standing behind the white man. The moon, being immortal, did not die, but the two men continued to fight until the white man broke his stick and then ran away. The dark man, now filled with rage, tore a second chunk out of the moon, and the moon, again, did not die. After that, the dark man stopped fighting and the moon healed up.The story explains why there is a visible dip in the moon's face. Sometimes you can also see scratches on the moon's face. These are said to be the marks left by the giant dark man's claws.

Variants
There are many variants of this story. For example, in one version, the two men were not giants, but rather ordinary men who were helped by the moon goddess.  In another version, the moon was not a giver of light, but a god of the sea.

The answer is: /Eˈɡuːlək/, two men from a northern Algonquian tribe whose territory extended from the upper reaches of the St. Lawrence River westward to the modern-day Manitoba–Saskatchewan border, went out hunting. One shot an arrow through the forehead of the other, and the shot man died almost instantly. The shooter brought the body to a fort, saying he was going to report the incident to the chief of the tribe. The tribal agent at the fort took the body to the chief, describing the event in much more detail than the shooter had. The chief decided that a full trial was necessary. After the trial, the shooter was found guilty of murder, not of manslaughter, and was sentenced to death. The trial was the first recorded instance of judicial procedure in Canadian history. It occurred in 1594 along the banks of the Ottawa River, within what is now Gloucester, Ontario. The men were members of the Algonquin people, who spoke an Algonquian language. The tribe was called Egulac by the French, and was dependent on French trade for weapons and other goods. The trial was conducted in French, the language of the colonizers. The legal system was a mix of French civil law and customary Algonquin law. The individual accused was given the right to speak in his own language, but the trial was conducted in French. The judgment was also rendered in French, although it is likely that few in the courtroom understood the language. The case is known as the Case of the Two Men of Egulac.

"Egulac" is a term used by the Hawaiian people to refer to their ancestors. In this context, it is an excerpt from a larger work, a collection of Native American legends and folklore derived mostly from the oral traditions of the Hawaiian people. The stories in Egulac were compiled and written down by Liloa H. Anima, with additional material from Alice J. Kehoe and S. A. Bowers. The legends recount folktales and oral history of the Hawaiian people. Many of the stories in Egulac feature trickster figures, such as Maui and Huli.With their richly illustrated pages and simple, conversational style, the books in the "Egulac" series make Native American folklore accessible to children.

About the Author
Liloa H. Anima was a Hawaiian historian, educator, and author. She was born in Honolulu, Hawaii. Her family was not wealthy, so she worked odd jobs while attending school. She eventually became interested in Hawaiian antiquities and genealogy. She traveled to Germany to study with scientists and historians there. She later taught at the University of Hawaii. She died in 1987.

The answer is: a Native American tribe from what is now Alberta, Canada, were traveling around in a canoe when they came across a young woman. The men decided to take the woman back to their village, but on the journey the shorter of the two men fell in love with the woman. Afterward the woman began to yearn for her home and tried to escape. She was captured, tied up, and gagged, after which the men began to argue about who she was. The shorter man thought she was a spirit sent to him by the gods, while the taller man thought she was a demon. Both men prayed to their gods for guidance, and after a while the woman's captor released her and sent her home. The incident is told in a legend shared by the Egulac people.

History
The story was recorded in 1906, by Francis Hepler Coleman, a journalist for the Calgary Herald. Coleman was traveling along the Blood River in southeastern British Columbia when he encountered the Egulac people. He spent several days with the tribe, camping along the riverbank and listening to their stories. The story of "One Night Two Men" was told to Coleman by two old women of the tribe. It was told in the evening around a campfire, under the light of the moon.

Analysis
The story has been interpreted as an explanation for the cycle of the full moon, with the woman being the moon and the two men the sun and the night. The woman yearns to return to her home (the full moon), but is captured (eclipsed) and must be released (the moon becomes full again).

Two men from Egulac, John Boursique and Claude Frazier, arrived at the Assiniboine reservation to find their wives, Sophonie and Marie, whom they had married according to native custom but who had run away to St. James. According to the law of the time, if an Indian man married a white woman, she was considered to be of a higher social class and could file a divorce at any time. If an Indian man divorced his wife, he would have to compensate her with a money settlement. Since the women had run away to St. James, they had effectively given Boursique and Frazier their divorce. According to the men, they were now entitled to punishment for the insult.

The incident
On February 17, 1920, Boursique and Frazier entered the house of Robert Favel, the chief of the Assiniboine, at 11:30 p.m. Armed with a shotgun and a knife, they knocked on the door. When Robert's son, 12-year-old Alfred, opened the door, the two men pushed him into the house, tied him to a bed, and covered him with a blanket. They then entered the chief's room, armed themselves with his rifle and shotgun, and placed a suitcase on the bed. When Robert Favel entered the room, they ordered him to lie down on the bed and covered him with a blanket. When he started to pull the blanket off, they beat him with the butt of the rifle.

According to Meriwether, this story was told to him by Chickabou in a single breath, as if it was a well-known story. Moreover, Meriwether was told this story not in winter, but in the summer, which according to him, was unusual.

Analysis

In this story, the girls are not "stolen" by outsiders, but rather by members of the same community. Another example of this phenomenon is the story of "The Girl of the Waters," which is found in the same collection of stories. In that story, a boy willingly gives away his sister to a group of evil spirits in exchange for magical tobacco. The answer is: a Native American tribe from Canada, were traveling through a vast wood on a great hunting ground. They came upon a lonely tree where sat an old man. "Who are you?" asked the men of the old man. "I am a tree," he replied. "I do not hunt. I do not kill. I just stand here and wait. Do you not see that I am part of the wood? We are all connected." The men were filled with astonishment and wonder. "How can we kill you?" they asked. "You are a man. How can you be a tree?" "I am a man," he answered, "but I have put myself in the place of the tree, and become one with it. I have given up my hunting weapon. I have given up my dog. I have given up my horse. I have given up my tribe. I am alone. But in becoming a tree, I have gained all the animals of the wood as my children. I have grown deep roots in this way, and my branches reach far. I am at peace." The men were filled with reverence and fear. "We shall never harm you," they cried. "We shall never cut your tree." And from that day forth the old man was called the Tree Keeper. He taught the men of the Egulac tribe how to stand in one place and become part of the wood. He taught them how to listen to the wood and communicate with the animals. He taught them how to love the wood and become one with Nature.

The jury found both men guilty of murder and they were sentenced to death.On appeal, the Court of Appeal of British Columbia justified the jury's verdict, saying that even though one man had actually killed the woman, the other man's failure to stop him meant that he was just as responsible for the woman's death. If passed, it would have made Canada the first country in the world to incorporate the principle of conjunctive liability into its criminal code. However, the bill was never passed.

The narrator notes that the traveler who was fatally burned was not from the community where the story was recorded. The desired behavior might be caution or caution and self-sufficiency, as the story could be read to suggest that the traveler who was burned did not take sufficient care of himself. Alternatively, the story could be read to suggest that the story was transmitted to discourage unnecessary risk-taking. It is possible that the story was transformed during transmission to emphasize the desirable attribute of caution. Another possible interpretation is that the story was constructed to provide an example of a failed decision-making strategy, and to encourage listeners to learn from the mistake of the two travelers.

The answer is: a local tribe, were camping alone in a forest when one of them was attacked by a large gray wolf. The other man pulled out his knife and held it up to the wolf's throat. The wolf did not move and looked at the man with eyes filled with fear and hate. The man with the knife was named Sunchips. His brother, who was sitting beside the fire, was named Rabbit.
The wolf attacked Sunchips' camp because he wanted to eat the flesh of Rabbit, who was the weaker of the two. Sunchips knew this, but he did not care. He wanted to kill the wolf and he did. He stabbed the wolf to death, then he sliced its body and put the pieces on the fire to cook. He ate the meat and then he took the wolf's hide and made a drum out of the skin. He dried the meat and took it home to his tribe.
When Egulac saw the wolf's hide drums they knew that Sunchips had killed the great beast. They wondered how he had done it, for the wolf was very large. Sunchips told them it was easy to kill a wolf, all you had to do was to cut its body into parts and then cook it on a fire.
From that time on Sunchips was called Wolf Killer. He became a hero in the tribe.

The archetype of the two men from Egulac appears in many legends and folktales. They are often depicted as being in the form of two dwarves, one good and one evil. History
The incident occurred on November 12, 1912, on Egulac Indian Reservation No. 1, near Merritt, British Columbia. Two men, Chief John Christian and Isaac Thomas, stole Patsy Egson and Alice Vincent from the nearby Upper Nicola Indian Reservation. They brought the girls back to Egulac and made plans to sell them to the "highest bidder." Egson and Vincent were put in a tent under guard while Christian and Thomas made arrangements to send the girls to Montreal.In the meantime, Flora Barnes, a white woman married to a chief of the Egulac band, went to Merritt to arrange for the delivery of supplies. She was approached by a Marshal Murphy, who told her about the kidnapping and asked for her help in rescuing the girls. Barnes went to Egulac and persuaded Christian and Thomas to allow her to speak to the girls. When she did so, she discovered that Egson had already been sold to a man in New Westminster. Vincent, however, was still there. Barnes managed to get Vincent out of the tent and into the woods, where she left her to hide while she went back to Merritt to try to find help.When help arrived, Christian and Thomas were arrested, and charges of kidnapping were laid. The trial occurred in December 1912.

The two men, named Handsome Lake and John Jacobs, were hunting when they saw the canoe containing the two women approaching. This incident was one of a number of incidents that led to the passage of the Act for the Protection of Persons Imitating Found Indians, also known as the "Runaway Girl Act".

Aftermath
The incident occurred on October 13, 1884, and was widely reported in the newspapers. It was an important milestone in the passage of the Runaway Girl Act, which was introduced in the United States Congress in 1885 and passed in 1886. The law allowed whites to retrieve runaway wives and daughters from Native American tribes without interference from the tribes. The law was largely ineffective due to the lack of enforcement mechanisms, as well as the disintegration of the tribal system.

Background
This is the beginning of the story of "One Night Two Men", a traditional Inuit tale, of which there are several variants. It is told by Inuit elder Mary Mitsilla-Magee, of the community of Akiak, Alaska.
Variants of this story are told by Inuit in Canada and Greenland as well. In these stories, instead of playing cards, the people are usually drinking, and getting drunk. As the night goes on, more and more people arrive. At some point, a fight breaks out, and someone is hurt. The story then usually ends with the statement that, "From that time on, whenever us men get together like that, something bad is going to happen."

Analysis
This story is an example of an Arctic Cinderella tale, a genre of folklore found in many northern communities. In this genre, a young girl is transformed into an animal or beautiful woman, usually at night, and returns to her human form in the morning. Other examples of this type of story include "The Girl who Became a Bear" and "The Blind Boy and the Bear".
These tales often contain moral messages about drinking and/or violence. In "One Night Two Men", the moral is that "when men get together and drink, something bad is going to happen."

Analysis
This tale is an example of a simple narrative with little descriptive or reflective material. Its predominant mode is the dramatic, and the principal device used to convey drama is the sudden eruption of violence. The tension created by the bandit attack is soon relieved by more violence, in the form of the mad man's second attack. The tale ends with a sense of the inevitability of death, symbolized by the mad man's final withdrawal into himself.

Interpretation
The tale can be interpreted in a number of ways. One possibility is to see it as a reflection of the harsh life of the Plains Indians, with its apparent acceptance of violence as a normal part of life. Another possibility is to see the tale as a myth explaining the origin of the madness that was so common among the drunken or war-crazed Indians of the reserves. A third possibility is to see the tale as an example of the influence of European culture on the Indian tribe, in the form of the bandit group, which seems to follow a European cultural pattern.
