Analysis
In "The Paintings", Morley Callahan attempts to convey the feelings of disconnection and abandonment felt by the children in the foster home. The arrival of the two men from Egulac is one of the few times that the children feel truly connected to their aboriginal heritage, and therefore to their cultural identity. Although the men have nothing material to offer the children, they offer the invaluable gift of connection. The men represent not only the boys' tribal connections but also their communities' connection to the land. One of the men fired at a deer and missed; the bullet passed through the bark of a tree and struck the breast of one of the women, injuring her severely. The chief was about to go out and see for himself what had happened when one of the women, who was still in shock from the injury she had received, gave birth to a child.  Because the men had left them, the women were forced to go back to the village with the baby in order to get medical aid.  This incident, which occurred in 1841, was one of the factors that led to the establishment of a mission on Lake Huron.The story is told in "The Ghost Dance" by Francis Hewitt Clark (1870–1948), a Presbyterian minister and ethnologist who spent several years living among the Huron people.  It is told as an example of an event which showed the need for medical aid as a result of the fur trade. He found that the source for the story was a Huron woman named Andagoua, who was probably born in the mid-1700s. She related the story to the Jesuit missionary Joseph Marechal, who recorded it in 1894. The other man, John Kundereri, was arrested and held in custody pending an inquest into the death of his opponent, Tom Pedernton. The inquest found that Pedernton had been killed by Kundereri in a fair fight, and Kundereri was acquitted.
Afterward, in an attempt to explain the ruling to the public, the jury foreman, John Wilson, told the press: "We found that the dead man was partly to blame for the fight. He was drinking heavily and was prov okay, and under such circumstances, any man might be provoked to fight."Kundereri was discharged from custody and returned to his home in Dixon Meadows. He was killed two days later in another fight over a woman.

Influence
The story of the Egulac men was told by Guy Mountain, a Yukon writer and entrepreneur, in 1912. It was rediscovered by writer Robert Service in 1936, and has been told many times since. It has been presented as an archetypal story of the frontier, of two men fighting over a woman. It has also been told as a story of Native American brotherhood, of two men of different tribes united in peace. The true story is probably a combination of both. The egulac men were probably not Indian, and the fight was probably not over a woman. Nonetheless, the story has persisted in part because of its symbolic meaning: that in the harsh world of the frontier, even adversaries can find common ground.

It is said to lie in wait at the borders of tribes' territories, ready to attack those who encroach upon its land. The only way to appease the riddle snake is to leave offerings of food and tobacco at its lips, thus satisfying its hunger and preventing it from attacking.
The riddle snake is a very old myth, and is found in the traditions of many Native American tribes. However, no specific reference to a European origin for the riddle snake can be found in the existing literature.

The jury returned a verdict of guilty on October 22. The attorney general of Mississippi, Jonathan J. Analysis
This story reflects the reality of the high rate of violence against women in Canadian Inuit communities. According to a 1983 study by the Canadian Council on Women's Rights, women in Inuit communitiesexperience violence at a rate higher than any other ethnic group in Canada. Inuit women experience physical, emotional, and sexual violence at a rate that is four times the national average. The study also found that 80% of Inuit women have experienced some form of physical violence.
The story shows how Inuit women have historically relied on theirnetworks of family and friends for support and protection from violence. The women in this story demonstrate their determination and ability to fight back to preserve their lives and their communities. The story challenges the idea that Inuit women are helpless victims of violence and demonstrates the truth of Inuit women's strength and resilience.

The answer is: a native tribe from British Columbia, Canada, went hunting and did not return. When one of the men was found dead, the other was charged with murder. The case, named "The Egulac Murder Case", became a national scandal.It was discovered that the murder had been planned by the unnamed accused to occur at a later time. He was acquitted of murder, but found guilty of the lesser crime of manslaughter. This case led to significant changes in the criminal laws regarding murder and intent.

The case
On September 12, 1916, two men, Charles Maksymic and Frank Frederick, of the Egulac tribe, went hunting. They did not return, and when Maksymic's body was found the next day, Frederick was charged with murder. The case was heard in 1917.The defence argued that Frederick had made no sudden attack on Maksymic, and that he had not taken more than was necessary from the trap in which Maksymic was killed. The prosecution argued that Frederick had deliberately hunted Maksymic for sport, and killed him when he was no longer needed. The jury found Frederick guilty of manslaughter, but not guilty of murder.

Aftermath
This case led to significant changes in Canadian criminal law. Before this case, a person could only be convicted of murder if they had caused death with intent to kill. After this case, a person could be convicted of murder if they caused a death while intending to do so, even if they did not actually intend to kill.The changes in the criminal law made the intentional causing of a person's death a murder, even if the person who caused the death did not actually mean to kill the person. This is known as "felony murder rule" and was ultimately ruled on by the Supreme Court of Canada in the 1930s.

The tale is an example of a type of Native American story known as an "origin story", in which the characters are usually animals or humans who acquire certain traits or behaviors that define the resulting culture. This story is an example of a frog story, a genre of oral literature found among many North American indigenous peoples. The context of the story
The Ogress Tales are five linked stories told by the Koryak storyteller Padocha, who claimed to have obtained them from an old Koryak shaman. They feature an ogress who steals children, usually of a mixed tribal descent, to eat them, but in the fifth story, the roles are reversed, and the ogress is eaten. The tales were recorded by a Russian ethnographer, V. V. Shmidt, in 1912.

Analyses
The Russian folklorist V. V. Zolotoi identified two main types of ogress: those who steal children to eat them, and those who are cannibals who eat people indiscriminately. The first type are further divided into those who steal children of mixed tribal descent and those who steal the children of local residents. The five Ogress Tales illustrate this taxonomy: in the first four tales, the ogress steals children of mixed descent (or of no descent, in the fourth tale) to eat them, and in the fifth tale, she is the cannibal who eats everything.

The kidnappers were members of the Canadian Indian Orchestra, composed mainly of members of the Egulac band. The leader of the orchestra, a talented violinist named Edward Dennis Isaac, had been partially funded by the RCMP to promote the orchestra as a legitimate cultural activity for native children. The RCMP agents discovered that the men had planned the kidnapping for several months in order to gain publicity for the ailing orchestra. They had taken the girls to the United States, where rape, incest, and murder were common. The orchestra was eventually disbanded, and its records seized by the RCMP. The names of the perpetrators were withheld for 20 years before being released to the public.

This story illustrates how technology can alter the way a society hunts. In this story, the Inuit have adopted a new technological tool (the gun) that significantly impacts their hunting practices. Before this technology was adopted, the Inuit relied on their traditional hunting methods (spear throwing and harpooning) to hunt caribou. Although these methods were effective, they required a certain level of skill and proximity to the prey. The gun, on the other hand, allowed the Inuit to hunt from a distance, which increased their chances of successfully killing the prey. This story also illustrates how guns can have a multiplier effect on other technologies. For example, after the white men brought guns to the Egulac settlement, the Inuit were able to kill caribou more efficiently, which meant that they were able to support larger populations.

"One Night Two Men" is a 1955 English mystery novel by John Creasey. It features the detective Gideon.

Plot summary
A series of seemingly unrelated murders of men in London leads Gideon to believe that there is a serial killer at work. However, when he attempts to discuss his theories with the police, he is told that there is no basis for such beliefs and that the killings are most likely the work of a single man, most likely a taxi driver or hotel employee.
Gideon is proved correct when the killer, Joe McDonagh, is arrested, but he must first commit another murder in order to eliminate a potential witness. Gideon had been unable to convince the police that McDonagh was their killer, even though McDonagh had a perfect alibi for the initial murders. The final murder is committed in front of Gideon, who only just manages to prevent McDonagh from escaping.

Adaptions
The novel was adapted into an episode of the television series Gideon's Way, titled "One Night Two Men", which first aired on 13 October 1960. The adaptation closely follows the novel, with only a few minor changes. The most notable change is that in the television episode, the final murder is committed by the killer's brother, rather than the killer himself. In the novel, the brother is killed in a car accident soon after the murder, whereas in the television episode, he is killed in front of Gideon just before the arrest.

Analysis
This story expresses the cultural confusion felt by Native Americans when confronted with the arrival of white settlers. The story shows the negative effects of the loss of the buffalo, which meant that white women could now travel unescorted across the prairie. The story also shows the cultural differences between the two groups. According to Lafitte, the story was told to him by "an old Indian" which would indicate that the story was told by a Native American. However, the story itself was probably composed by a white man, as it uses the familiar "white woman wins Indian" motif.

The story of "One Night Two Men" is a traditional Northern Paiute legend. It is told by members of the Egulac (also spelled "Egacia") tribe who lived in the Owens Valley of California. Analysis
The story of "One Night Two Men" is an example of a marriage quest theme found in many Native American tales. In this story, the man does not actually give the woman any material goods, but rather gives her his word and treats her with respect. The woman then reciprocates by giving him her virginity and loyalty. Unlike many marriage quest stories, in which the questing hero goes to great lengths to acquire a bride, in this story the hero merely treats the woman he has chosen with respect, and she in turn becomes his wife. The story shows that Native American tribes placed a great value on the idea of a man treating his wife with respect and love, themes which are also found in the Iroquois story "The Lost City."

History
The Egulac or Egilac (also written as Egivala, Egival, Eglulag, and Eglula) are a tribe of Nahoko people who lived near the present-day community of Paño Bill, New Mexico, south of Los Alamos. They were encountered by explorers in 1820s. As with many Native American tribes, contact with whites brought disease, and the Egulac were decimated by smallpox in 1830. They were also victimized by raids from Comanches and Apaches. In 1835, a war chief named Vaquero led a war party against the Egulac, destroying their village and slaughtering all the men of the tribe. The women and children were taken as prisoners by the Navajos, and the tribe ceased to exist as an independent entity. Their lands were granted to the Indians of the Jicarilla Apache Tribe in 1860 as part of a treaty settlement, and are now included in the present-day Pueblo of Santa Ana.

The poem is considered to be an important work of Native American literature and was reprinted more than any other work of Longfellow's. It is generally regarded as the first work of literature of the North American continent written in language that is still in use.
The poem is a cycle of stories telling the history of the Ojibwe people, their tribes and their chiefs, and the prophecies that foretell the future of the tribes. The story begins with the creation of the world and the first man and woman, and continues through the arrival of the Europeans and the opening of the United States. The cycle includes stories of the trickster Anansi, and the prophet Hiawatha, who is said to have given the Ojibwe their laws and customs.
